panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Frontal clinical photograph of Patient 1 with multiple captioned characteristic dysmorphic facial manifestations of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. B: Frontal clinical photograph of Patient 2 with captioned dysmorphic facial features associated with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. C: Profile clinical photograph of Patient 1 demonstrating the facial dysmorphism specified in the caption for 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. D: Profile clinical photograph of Patient 2 showing captioned dysmorphic facial features of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

panels.figure_caption: Front and profile photographs of 2 patients with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, illustrating characteristic dysmorphic features. Patient 1 (left) exhibits amimic face, widow's peak, protruding ears, hooded or puffy upper eyelids, a broad tubular nose with a bulbous tip, low‐set ears, microstomia, and retrognathia. Patient 2 (right) shows a lengthened upper face, hooded or puffy upper eyelids, a broad tubular nose, and malar flattening.
in_text_mentions: The first patient had mild intellectual disability, facial anomalies (Fig. 1), and delayed psychomotor development. He attended specialized schooling, later obtained vocational training, and entered the workforce. At age 32, he developed a right‐sided resting tremor and was diagnosed with PD, with good dopaminergic responsiveness. At age 34, he developed motor fluctuations. At age 35, during treatment adjustment, he developed hallucinations, delusions, and agitation requiring clozapine.

The second patient had, in addition to facial anomalies (Fig. 1; Table 1), childhood learning difficulties and left school early but later completed vocational training. During adolescence, he developed anxiety followed by heavy alcohol and cannabis use. Persistent psychotic symptoms led to a diagnosis of schizophrenia at age 37, treated with clozapine.
